questions.q: For which real number k is (k + 2i)/(1 − i) a real number?
questions.x: Multiply top and bottom by 1 + i: (k + 2i)(1 + i)/2 = ((k − 2) + (k + 2)i)/2. This is real when k + 2 = 0, so k = −2 (the number is then −2). k = 2 makes it purely imaginary instead.

questions.q: What is the additive inverse of the complex number −2 + 5i?
questions.x: The additive inverse w satisfies z + w = 0, so w = −z = 2 − 5i. −2 − 5i is the conjugate and (−2 − 5i)/29 is the multiplicative inverse.

questions.q: The graph of y = x² is shifted 2 units to the right and then 3 units up. What is the equation of the new graph?
questions.x: Moving right 2 replaces x by x − 2 and moving up 3 adds 3: y = (x − 2)² + 3 = x² − 4x + 7, with vertex (2, 3). Replacing x by x + 2 would move the graph left.

questions.q: If log x = 2 log 3 − log 6 + log 4 (common logarithms), what is x?
questions.x: 2 log 3 = log 9, so the right side is log(9 × 4 / 6) = log 6, giving x = 6. Dropping the logs and working out 2·3 − 6 + 4 gives 4.

questions.q: lim(x→∞) (3ˣ + 2ˣ)/(3ˣ − 2ˣ) equals:
questions.x: Divide top and bottom by 3ˣ: (1 + (2/3)ˣ)/(1 − (2/3)ˣ). As x → ∞, (2/3)ˣ → 0, so the limit is 1. (As x → −∞ the limit would be −1.)

questions.q: Gaussian elimination is applied to x + 3y = 5, 2x + y = 0, using R₂ → R₂ − 2R₁ on the augmented matrix. What is the solution?
questions.x: R₂ − 2R₁ turns (2, 1 | 0) into (0, −5 | −10), so y = 2; back-substitution gives x = 5 − 3(2) = −1. Check: −1 + 6 = 5 and 2(−1) + 2 = 0.

questions.q: When a polynomial f(x) is divided by x² − 1, the remainder is 3x + 2. What is the remainder when f(x) is divided by x + 1?
questions.x: f(x) = (x² − 1)q(x) + 3x + 2, and x² − 1 is zero at x = −1. So the remainder on division by x + 1 is f(−1) = 3(−1) + 2 = −1. Using x = 1 instead gives 5, the remainder for x − 1.

questions.q: What is the greatest value of f(x) = 5 + 4x − x², and for which x does it occur?
questions.x: f(x) = −(x² − 4x) + 5 = −(x − 2)² + 4 + 5 = 9 − (x − 2)², so the greatest value is 9 at x = 2. Check: f(2) = 5 + 8 − 4 = 9. A sign slip in the completed square gives x = −2.

questions.q: Resolve 5x/((x − 1)(x² + 4)) into partial fractions.
questions.x: 5x = A(x² + 4) + (Bx + C)(x − 1). x = 1 gives 5 = 5A, A = 1; x² terms: A + B = 0, B = −1; constants: 4A − C = 0, C = 4. Check at x = 0: 0 = 1/(−1) + 4/4. The other forms fail this check.

questions.q: What is the sum of the infinite series 1 + 3/2 + 5/4 + 7/8 + … ?
questions.x: S = 1 + 3x + 5x² + … with x = 1/2. Then S − xS = 1 + 2x + 2x² + … = 1 + 2x/(1 − x), so S(1 − x) = 1 + 2 = 3 and S = 3/(1/2) = 6. Check with the formula (1 + x)/(1 − x)² = 1.5/0.25 = 6. Stopping at S(1 − x) = 3 gives 3.

questions.q: In how many ways can 12 students be split into one group of 8 and one group of 4?
questions.x: Choosing the 4 for the small group fixes the other 8: C(12, 4) = (12 × 11 × 10 × 9)/24 = 495. This is the same as C(12, 8). Doubling it for the two groups gives 990, but the groups have different sizes, so nothing is counted twice.

questions.q: A letter is chosen at random from the letters of the word STATISTICS. What is the probability that it is T?
questions.x: STATISTICS has 10 letters and 3 of them are T, so the probability is 3/10. Dividing by the 5 different letters or by the 7 non-T letters gives the wrong options.

questions.q: For |x| < 1, the first three terms of the expansion of ∛(1 − x) are:
questions.x: (1 + y)^(1/3) = 1 + y/3 + (1/3)(−2/3)/2 · y² = 1 + y/3 − y²/9. With y = −x: 1 − x/3 − x²/9 (y² = x² stays positive). Forgetting to divide by 2! gives −2x²/9.

questions.q: One radian, expressed in degrees, is approximately:
questions.x: 1 rad = 180°/π ≈ 57.3° (about 57°17′45″). 0.0175 is the size of 1° in radians, the reverse conversion.

questions.q: What is the value of 8 sin 15° cos 15° cos 30°?
questions.x: 2 sin 15° cos 15° = sin 30°, so the expression is 4 sin 30° cos 30° = 2 sin 60° = √3. Using sin 2θ = sin θ cos θ (no factor 2) gives √3/2.

questions.q: What is the difference between the greatest and least values of y = 12 sin x − 5 cos x?
questions.x: 12 sin x − 5 cos x = 13 sin(x − φ) with 13 = √(144 + 25), so y runs from −13 to 13 and the difference is 26. 13 is only the greatest value, and 17 and 7 come from adding or subtracting the coefficients.

questions.q: A vertical pole casts a shadow 12 m long on level ground when the sun's elevation is 60°. How long is its shadow when the elevation is 30°?
questions.x: Height = 12 tan 60° = 12√3 m. At 30°, shadow = 12√3 ÷ tan 30° = 12√3 × √3 = 36 m. 12√3 m is the height of the pole, not the new shadow.

questions.q: For x > −1, tan⁻¹((x − 1)/(x + 1)) equals:
questions.x: By the subtraction formula, tan⁻¹x − tan⁻¹1 = tan⁻¹((x − 1)/(1 + x)), and for x > −1 the angle tan⁻¹x − π/4 lies in (−π/2, π/4), inside the principal range. Check x = 1: tan⁻¹0 = 0 = π/4 − π/4.

questions.q: The solutions of sin 3θ = −1 in the interval 0 ≤ θ < 2π are:
questions.x: 3θ = 3π/2 + 2nπ, so θ = π/2 + 2nπ/3, giving π/2, 7π/6, 11π/6 in [0, 2π). Check 7π/6: sin(7π/2) = −1. The set π/6, 5π/6, 3π/2 solves sin 3θ = +1.

questions.q: If f(x) = (x − 1)(x − 2)(x − 3), what is f′(2)?
questions.x: By the product rule, every term containing the factor (x − 2) vanishes at x = 2, leaving (2 − 1)(2 − 3) = −1. Check: f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 11x − 6, f′(2) = 12 − 24 + 11 = −1. The answer 0 confuses f(2) = 0 with f′(2).

questions.q: What is the derivative of y = 1/√(2x + 1), x > −1/2?
∫ (ln x)/√x dx, for x > 0, equals:
questions.x: Take u = ln x, dv = x^(−1/2) dx, v = 2√x: 2√x ln x − ∫2√x (1/x) dx = 2√x ln x − ∫2x^(−1/2) dx = 2√x ln x − 4√x + C.

questions.q: ∫ (x + 2)/(x² + 4x + 3) dx, for x > −1, equals:
questions.x: The numerator is half the derivative of the denominator (2x + 4), so the integral is ½ ln(x² + 4x + 3) + C. Partial fractions agree: (x + 2)/((x + 1)(x + 3)) = ½/(x + 1) + ½/(x + 3).

questions.q: If dy/dx = √(1 − y²) and y = 0 when x = 0, what is y when x = π/6?
questions.x: Separate: dy/√(1 − y²) = dx, so sin⁻¹y = x + c; y(0) = 0 gives c = 0. Then y = sin x and y(π/6) = ½. Integrating to cos⁻¹y by mistake leads to √3/2.

questions.q: What is the area of the triangle with vertices (1, 1), (4, 2) and (2, 5)?
A line through (1, 4) makes a triangle of area 8 with the positive coordinate axes. What is its equation?
questions.x: With x/a + y/b = 1: 1/a + 4/b = 1 and ab = 16. Putting b = 16/a gives a² − 4a + 4 = 0, so a = 2, b = 8 and the line is 4x + y − 8 = 0. Check: 2x + y − 6 = 0 and x + y − 5 = 0 also pass through (1, 4) but give areas 9 and 12.5.

questions.q: At which points do the parabolas y² = 4x and x² = 4y meet?
questions.x: From x² = 4y, y = x²/4; then x⁴/16 = 4x gives x(x³ − 64) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 4: the points (0, 0) and (4, 4). Check: 16 = 4 × 4 in both equations.

questions.q: The line lx + my + n = 0 (l, m ≠ 0) touches the parabola y² = 4ax. Which condition holds?
questions.x: Write the line as y = −(l/m)x − n/m. A line y = kx + c touches y² = 4ax when c = a/k, so −n/m = −am/l, giving am² = ln. Check: x − y + 1 = 0 touches y² = 4x (a = 1, l = 1, m = −1, n = 1: 1 = 1).

questions.q: A projectile has position r(t) = 3t i + (4t − 5t²) j. What is its speed at the instant its velocity is horizontal?
questions.x: v = 3i + (4 − 10t)j is horizontal when t = 0.4, and then v = 3i, so the speed is 3. 5 is the starting speed √(9 + 16).

questions.q: What are the direction cosines of the vector 2i − 3j + 6k?
questions.x: |v| = √(4 + 9 + 36) = 7, so the direction cosines are 2/7, −3/7, 6/7. Check: their squares add to 49/49 = 1. Dividing by 2 + 3 + 6 = 11 instead of the magnitude gives the last triple.

questions.q: A rope measured as 7.0 m long is cut into exactly 3 equal pieces. The length of each piece, written to the correct number of significant figures, is:
questions.x: The 3 is an exact count, so it does not limit the significant figures; the result keeps the two of 7.0 m: 7.0/3 = 2.33… → 2.3 m. Treating 3 as a one-figure measurement gives the tempting 2 m.

questions.q: Which of these is a source of random error in a set of readings?
o: A zero error in a screw gauge
A stopwatch that always runs slow
Small unpredictable changes in room temperature while the readings are taken
A metre rule whose zero end is worn away
questions.x: Random errors vary unpredictably from reading to reading, like small fluctuations in the surroundings, and they scatter readings on both sides of the true value. The other three shift every reading the same way, so they are systematic errors.

questions.q: A picture hangs at rest from a nail by a string whose two halves make equal angles with the vertical. If a shorter string is used, so that the angle between the two halves increases, the tension in the string:
questions.x: Vertically, 2T cos(θ/2) = W, where θ is the angle between the halves. As θ increases cos(θ/2) falls, so T = W/[2 cos(θ/2)] increases. Thinking a shorter string carries less load gives the wrong answer.

questions.q: A projectile is launched from level ground so that its horizontal range is four times its maximum height. Ignoring air resistance, its angle of projection above the horizontal is:
questions.x: R = 2v² sin θ cos θ/g and H = v² sin²θ/2g, so R/H = 4 cos θ/sin θ = 4/tan θ. R = 4H gives tan θ = 1, θ = 45°. Check at 45°: R = v²/g and H = v²/4g, ratio 4.

questions.q: A stone is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹ from the top of a tower 25 m high. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 10 m s⁻², it reaches the ground at the foot of the tower after:
questions.x: Taking up as positive: −25 = 20t − 5t², so t² − 4t − 5 = 0 and t = 5 s. Check: it rises for 2 s to 20 m above the top (45 m above ground), then falls 45 m in 3 s; total 5 s. 4 s is only the time to come back to the top of the tower.

questions.q: With g the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of a planet of radius R, the escape velocity from its surface is:
questions.x: Since GM = gR², v = √(2GM/R) = √(2gR²/R) = √(2gR). √(gR) is the speed of a satellite orbiting close to the surface, which lacks the factor 2.

questions.q: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, how are its angular velocity and the linear velocity of a point on the body (not on the axis) related in direction?
o: They are parallel to each other
They are perpendicular to each other
They are inclined at 45° to each other
questions.x: Angular velocity points along the axis (right-hand rule), while the linear velocity of a point is tangent to its circle, which lies in a plane perpendicular to the axis. So they are perpendicular (v = ω × r).

questions.q: A body moves in a circle at constant speed. Its centripetal acceleration is:
o: Constant in both magnitude and direction
Zero, because the speed is constant
Constant in magnitude but changing in direction
Changing in magnitude but fixed in direction
questions.x: a = v²/r has a fixed size, but it always points to the centre, so its direction keeps turning with the body. Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration, because the velocity's direction changes.

questions.q: A solid loses 2.0 N of its weight when completely immersed in water (density 1000 kg m⁻³), and 1.6 N when completely immersed in an oil. The density of the oil is:
questions.x: The loss of weight is the upthrust ρVg, and V is the same in both liquids, so ρ_oil/ρ_water = 1.6/2.0 and ρ_oil = 0.8 × 1000 = 800 kg m⁻³. Inverting the ratio gives 1250 kg m⁻³.

questions.q: A simple pendulum moves with simple harmonic motion only when its amplitude is small, because only then:
o: The tension in the string equals the weight of the bob
Air resistance on the bob can be ignored
The string stays straight and does not stretch
sin θ ≈ θ (in radians), so the restoring force is proportional to the displacement
questions.x: The restoring force is mg sin θ. Only for small θ is sin θ ≈ θ = x/l, giving F = −(mg/l)x, which is the SHM condition F ∝ −x. Tension and air resistance do not decide whether the motion is SHM.

questions.q: A string 0.8 m long, of mass per unit length 0.01 kg m⁻¹, is fixed at both ends and stretched by a tension of 64 N. Its fundamental frequency is:
questions.x: Wave speed v = √(F/μ) = √(64/0.01) = √6400 = 80 m s⁻¹; fundamental f₁ = v/2L = 80/1.6 = 50 Hz. Using v/L gives 100 Hz; forgetting the square root gives 4000 Hz.

questions.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ falls on polaroid P. Polaroid Q follows, with its axis at 30° to that of P, and polaroid R follows Q, with its axis at 90° to that of P. What intensity comes out of R?
questions.x: After P: I₀/2. After Q (30°): I₀/2 × cos² 30° = I₀/2 × 3/4 = 3I₀/8. Q and R are 60° apart, so after R: 3I₀/8 × cos² 60° = 3I₀/8 × 1/4 = 3I₀/32. Forgetting the first halving gives 3I₀/16; treating P and R as crossed with nothing between gives zero.

questions.q: A single slit is lit first with blue light and then with red light, with everything else unchanged. Compared with blue light, the central bright band with red light is:
o: Wider, because the angle of the first minimum increases with wavelength
Narrower, because red light has a longer wavelength
The same width, because the slit is unchanged
Wider, because red light has a higher frequency
questions.x: The first minimum is at sin θ = λ/a, so a longer wavelength gives a larger angle and a wider central band. Red light has a lower frequency than blue, not a higher one.

questions.q: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. The eyepiece is adjusted so that the final image is at the near point, 25 cm from the eye held close to the eyepiece. What is the magnifying power?
questions.x: For the eyepiece, 1/u = 1/5 + 1/25 = 6/25, so the intermediate image is 25/6 cm from it. The angular magnification is fₒ/u = 100 × 6/25 = 24, the same as (fₒ/fₑ)(1 + fₑ/d) = 20 × 1.2. Using normal adjustment gives 20.

questions.q: An ideal gas in an insulated container expands freely into a vacuum. No heat enters and no work is done. The entropy of the gas:
o: Stays the same, because no heat enters
Increases, because the process is irreversible
questions.x: A free expansion is irreversible: the gas spreads into a larger volume and becomes more disordered, so its entropy rises even though Q = 0. ΔS = Q/T applies only along a reversible path, which is the slip behind 'stays the same'.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands isothermally. The change in its internal energy is:
o: Equal to the work done by the gas
Equal to the heat it absorbs
Negative, because the gas does work
questions.x: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, which is constant in an isothermal process, so ΔU = 0. The heat absorbed equals the work done by the gas, but neither is the change in internal energy.

questions.q: A charge of 5 μC is moved 3 m along an equipotential surface that is at 100 V. The work done by the electric field is:
questions.x: W = qΔV, and ΔV = 0 between two points on the same equipotential surface, so no work is done. Multiplying the charge by the 100 V level gives 0.5 mJ, which is the slip.

questions.q: How many electrons must be removed from a neutral metal sphere to give it a charge of +1.6 μC? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
questions.x: n = q/e = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1 × 10¹³. Taking μC as mC gives 1 × 10¹⁶.

questions.q: The current in a wire rises uniformly from 0 to 4 A in 10 s. The charge that passes a cross-section of the wire in these 10 s is:
questions.x: Charge is the area under the current-time graph: a triangle, ½ × 10 s × 4 A = 20 C. The same follows from the average current 2 A × 10 s. Forgetting the ½ gives 40 C.

questions.q: A moving-coil galvanometer has a rectangular coil of 100 turns, 4 cm × 5 cm, in a radial magnetic field of 0.5 T. The suspension's torsion constant (couple per unit twist) is 2 × 10⁻⁵ N m rad⁻¹. The current that gives a deflection of 0.5 rad is:
questions.x: At equilibrium NIAB = cθ. A = 20 cm² = 2 × 10⁻³ m², so I = cθ/(NAB) = (2 × 10⁻⁵ × 0.5)/(100 × 2 × 10⁻³ × 0.5) = 10⁻⁵/0.1 = 1 × 10⁻⁴ A. Leaving out θ gives 2 × 10⁻⁴ A.

questions.q: A galvanometer gives full-scale deflection with a current of 50 μA. When it is made into a voltmeter, the voltmeter's resistance per volt of its range (its 'ohms per volt') is:
questions.x: For a range V, the total resistance is V/Ig, so the resistance per volt is 1/Ig = 1/(50 × 10⁻⁶) = 20 000 Ω V⁻¹ = 20 kΩ V⁻¹. Writing μA as 10⁻⁵ A gives 2 kΩ V⁻¹.

questions.q: A straight conductor of length L moves at speed v along the direction of its own length through a uniform magnetic field B that is at right angles to the conductor. The emf induced between its ends is:
questions.x: Moving along its own length, the conductor cuts no field lines: the magnetic force on its charges (along v × B) is at right angles to the rod, so no charge is pushed along it and no emf appears. BLv needs L, v and B mutually perpendicular.

questions.q: The reactance of an inductor, XL, and of a capacitor, XC, are each plotted against the frequency f of the supply. Which description is correct?
o: XL falls in inverse proportion to f; XC is a straight line through the origin
Both are straight lines through the origin
Both are horizontal lines, independent of frequency
XL is a straight line through the origin; XC falls in inverse proportion to f
questions.x: XL = 2πfL is directly proportional to f, a straight line through the origin, while XC = 1/(2πfC) is inversely proportional to f, a curve that falls as f rises. Swapping the two is the usual slip.

questions.q: When a superconductor is cooled below its critical temperature in a magnetic field, it pushes the magnetic field lines out of itself (the Meissner effect). In this state it behaves as:
o: An ordinary conductor with low resistance
questions.x: Expelling all magnetic flux means the field inside is zero, which is perfect diamagnetism; this is why a small magnet can float above a cooled superconductor. Ferro- and paramagnets draw field lines in, not out.

questions.q: A non-inverting amplifier has a 1 kΩ resistor between the inverting input and earth. For a voltage gain of 11, the feedback resistor must be:
questions.x: For a non-inverting amplifier, gain = 1 + R₂/R₁, so 11 = 1 + R₂/1 kΩ and R₂ = 10 kΩ. Using the inverting formula R₂/R₁ = 11 gives 11 kΩ.

questions.q: A square plate of side 1 m at rest moves at 0.6c in a direction parallel to one pair of its sides. The area of the plate measured by a stationary observer is:
questions.x: Only the side along the motion contracts: L = 1 × √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8 m, while the perpendicular side stays 1 m, so the area is 0.8 × 1 = 0.8 m². Contracting both sides gives 0.64 m²; dividing by 0.8 instead of multiplying gives 1.25 m².

questions.q: An electron and a proton have the same de Broglie wavelength. They must have the same:
questions.x: λ = h/p, so equal wavelengths mean equal momenta. Since the proton is about 1836 times heavier, its speed must be correspondingly smaller, and its kinetic energy p²/2m is also smaller.

questions.q: A laser tube has a mirror at each end, one fully reflecting and one partly reflecting. The purpose of the mirrors is to:
o: Produce the population inversion by heating the gas
Change the wavelength of the light at each reflection
Send photons back and forth through the medium to cause more stimulated emission, letting part of the beam out through the partial mirror
questions.x: Each pass through the excited medium produces more stimulated photons in the same direction, so the light builds up (amplification); the partly reflecting mirror lets a fraction out as the beam. The population inversion is produced by pumping, not by the mirrors, and reflection does not change the wavelength.

questions.q: A nucleus of ²³⁸₉₂U emits one alpha particle and then two beta (β⁻) particles one after the other. The final nucleus is:
questions.x: The alpha decay gives ²³⁴₉₀Th (A − 4, Z − 2); each β⁻ raises Z by 1 and leaves A unchanged, so Z goes 90 → 92 and the product is ²³⁴₉₂U, an isotope of the parent. Stopping after the alpha decay gives ²³⁴₉₀Th; taking 4 more off A for the beta decays gives ²³⁰₉₂U, and raising Z by 2 for each β⁻ gives Z = 94.

questions.q: In β⁺ (positron) decay, a proton in the nucleus changes into a neutron. At the quark level:
o: A down quark changes into an up quark
An up quark changes into a strange quark
An up quark changes into a down quark
questions.x: Proton (u u d) → neutron (u d d), so one u (+⅔e) becomes a d (−⅓e); the lost charge +e is carried off by the positron, with an electron neutrino. d → u is what happens in β⁻ decay.

questions.q: How many moles of ions in total are present in 11.1 g of calcium chloride, CaCl₂? (Ca = 40, Cl = 35.5)
questions.x: Molar mass of CaCl₂ = 40 + 71 = 111 g mol⁻¹, so 11.1 g is 0.1 mol. Each formula unit gives one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻, i.e. 3 ions, so 0.3 mol of ions. 0.1 mol counts formula units only and 0.2 mol counts only the Cl⁻ ions.

questions.q: What is the mass of 0.25 mol of calcium carbonate, CaCO₃? (C = 12, O = 16, Ca = 40)
questions.x: Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 40 + 12 + 48 = 100 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.25 × 100 = 25 g. 100 g is the molar mass itself, and dividing instead of multiplying gives a far too small value.

questions.q: Hydrogen is collected over water at 25 °C when the total pressure is 760 mm Hg. The vapour pressure of water at 25 °C is 24 mm Hg. The pressure of the dry hydrogen is:
questions.x: By Dalton's law, P(total) = P(H₂) + P(water vapour), so P(H₂) = 760 − 24 = 736 mm Hg. Adding the vapour pressure instead of subtracting it gives 784 mm Hg.

questions.q: A metal crystallises in a body-centred cubic unit cell, with an atom at each corner and one at the centre of the cube. The number of atoms belonging to one unit cell is:
questions.x: Each corner atom is shared by 8 cells: 8 × ⅛ = 1, plus 1 whole atom at the centre = 2. Counting all nine atoms as whole gives 9; 4 is the count for a face-centred cubic cell.

questions.q: The charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) of a proton is 9.58 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹. Taking the mass of an alpha particle as four times that of a proton, the e/m of an alpha particle is about:
questions.x: An alpha particle (He²⁺) has twice the charge and four times the mass of a proton, so its e/m = (2/4) × 9.58 × 10⁷ = 4.79 × 10⁷ C kg⁻¹. Forgetting the double charge gives one-quarter (2.40 × 10⁷).

questions.q: The maximum number of electrons in an atom that can have n = 3 and l = 1 is:
questions.x: n = 3, l = 1 is the 3p subshell, with m = −1, 0, +1 (three orbitals) holding 2 electrons each = 6. 18 is the capacity of the whole n = 3 shell and 10 is the 3d subshell.

questions.q: Which molecule is polar even though its central atom has no lone pair?
questions.x: In CH₂Cl₂ the carbon is tetrahedral with no lone pair, but two C–Cl and two C–H bond dipoles are unequal and do not cancel, so the molecule has a dipole moment. CCl₄, BF₃ and BeCl₂ are symmetrical with identical bonds, so their bond dipoles cancel. Thinking 'tetrahedral means non-polar' leads to rejecting CH₂Cl₂.

questions.q: Given N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g), ΔH = +66 kJ, and N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) → N₂O₄(g), ΔH = +9 kJ, what is ΔH for 2NO₂(g) → N₂O₄(g)?
questions.x: Reverse the first equation (2NO₂ → N₂ + 2O₂, ΔH = −66 kJ) and add the second: ΔH = −66 + 9 = −57 kJ. +57 reverses the wrong equation, and +75 adds the two values without reversing either.

questions.q: Argon is added to an equilibrium mixture of N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) while the total pressure is kept constant, so the volume of the container increases. What happens to the amount of NO₂?
o: It decreases, because the argon raises the pressure
It increases, because the partial pressures fall and the equilibrium shifts to the side with more gas molecules
It stays the same, because argon does not take part in the reaction
It stays the same, because the total pressure is unchanged
questions.x: At constant total pressure the volume grows, so the partial pressures of N₂O₄ and NO₂ fall, just as if the mixture were expanded; the system shifts towards more gas molecules, forming more NO₂. 'Stays the same' is correct only when argon is added at constant volume.

questions.q: In the equilibrium N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) at a certain temperature, the total pressure is 2.0 atm and the mole fraction of NO₂ is 0.50. What is Kp?
questions.x: Partial pressure = mole fraction × total pressure, so p(NO₂) = 0.50 × 2.0 = 1.0 atm and p(N₂O₄) = 1.0 atm. Kp = p(NO₂)² / p(N₂O₄) = 1.0 ÷ 1.0 = 1.0 atm. Using the mole fractions directly as pressures gives 0.25 ÷ 0.50 = 0.50.

questions.q: What is the approximate pH of 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ mol dm⁻³ hydrochloric acid at 25 °C?
questions.x: The H⁺ from the acid (10⁻⁸) is much smaller than the 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³ provided by the ionisation of water, so both must be counted: [H⁺] is about 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ and the pH is just below 7 (about 6.98). An acid solution cannot have pH 8; that answer comes from using −log(10⁻⁸) without thinking.

questions.q: A solution labelled 0.25 mol kg⁻¹ (molal) in NaCl contains 0.25 mol of NaCl in each:
questions.x: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, here water. Moles per dm³ of solution is molarity, the most common mix-up.

questions.q: Using E°: Li⁺/Li = −3.04 V, Mg²⁺/Mg = −2.37 V, Zn²⁺/Zn = −0.76 V, Cu²⁺/Cu = +0.34 V, which metal is the strongest reducing agent?
questions.x: The most negative reduction potential means the metal gives up electrons most readily, so lithium is the strongest reducing agent. Copper, with the most positive E°, is the weakest; picking it is the usual sign mix-up.

questions.q: A reaction is zero order with k = 0.010 mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. If the initial concentration of the reactant is 0.50 mol dm⁻³, how long does it take for the reactant to be used up completely?
questions.x: For zero order the concentration falls at a constant rate k: 0.50/0.010 = 50 s. 25 s is only the half-life, and 69.3 s comes from wrongly using the first-order formula 0.693/k.

questions.q: An element X forms the ion X²⁺, whose electronic configuration is the same as that of argon. Where is X in the periodic table?
questions.x: X has two more electrons than argon (18), so Z = 20, calcium: [Ar] 4s², period 4, group 2. Mg²⁺ has the neon configuration, and a period 3, group 16 element (S) gets the argon configuration by gaining electrons, not losing them.

questions.q: In the Nelson cell for the manufacture of sodium hydroxide from brine, which gases are given off at the electrodes?
o: Hydrogen at the graphite anode, chlorine at the steel cathode
Oxygen at the graphite anode, hydrogen at the steel cathode
Chlorine at the graphite anode, hydrogen at the steel cathode
Chlorine at the graphite anode, oxygen at the steel cathode
questions.x: Cl⁻ ions from the concentrated brine are oxidised at the anode to chlorine; water is reduced at the cathode to hydrogen, leaving OH⁻ that forms NaOH with Na⁺. Swapping the electrodes is the common slip.

questions.q: Silicones are used to make fabrics and masonry water-repellent mainly because:
o: They react with water to form insoluble silica
Their Si–O bonds form hydrogen bonds with water and hold it
They are ionic solids that do not dissolve in water
Their non-polar alkyl groups face outward around the Si–O–Si backbone and repel water
questions.x: A silicone has an Si–O–Si backbone with methyl (or other alkyl) groups on silicon; these hydrocarbon groups on the outside are non-polar, so water is not attracted and runs off. Silicones are covalent polymers and are chemically inert to water, so the hydrolysis option is wrong.

questions.q: In waterlogged soil, some bacteria convert nitrate ions into nitrogen gas, which returns to the atmosphere. This step of the nitrogen cycle is called:
questions.x: Denitrifying bacteria in oxygen-poor soil reduce NO₃⁻ to N₂. Nitrification is the opposite direction (NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻), and fixation turns N₂ into compounds, so nitrification is the tempting mix-up.

questions.q: Which halogen reacts rapidly with cold water, oxidising it to oxygen gas and forming its hydrogen halide as the only other product?
questions.x: Fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent: 2F₂ + 2H₂O → 4HF + O₂. Chlorine instead gives HCl and HOCl (Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HOCl), so it does not fit the stem, and bromine and iodine are weaker still.

questions.q: The oxides CrO, Cr₂O₃ and CrO₃ are, respectively:
questions.x: Chromium is +2, +3 and +6 in these oxides; as the oxidation state rises the metal becomes more like a non-metal, so the oxide changes from basic (CrO) to amphoteric (Cr₂O₃) to acidic (CrO₃, which gives chromic acid). Reversing the trend is the usual slip.

questions.q: The functional group –CONH₂ is found in:
questions.x: –CONH₂ is a carbonyl group bonded to nitrogen, the amide group (e.g. ethanamide, CH₃CONH₂). Amines have –NH₂ without the C=O, which makes them the tempting confusion.

questions.q: 1,2-Dibromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₂Br, is warmed with zinc dust in ethanol. The organic product is:
questions.x: Zinc removes the two bromine atoms from neighbouring carbons (dehalogenation) and a C=C forms: CH₃CHBrCH₂Br + Zn → CH₃CH=CH₂ + ZnBr₂. Propyne would need two molecules of HBr removed by alcoholic KOH.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride, CH₃COCl, in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The electrophile that attacks the ring is:
questions.x: AlCl₃ removes Cl⁻ from CH₃COCl: CH₃COCl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CO⁺ + AlCl₄⁻. The acylium ion attacks the ring. AlCl₄⁻ is a by-product and is negative, so it cannot be an electrophile; CH₃⁺ would need chloromethane.

questions.q: Which reaction gives 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CCl, as the main product?
questions.x: HCl adds to (CH₃)₂C=CH₂ by Markovnikov's rule, putting Cl on the carbon with two methyl groups. SOCl₂ keeps the chlorine where the OH was, giving 1-chloro-2-methylpropane; but-1-ene gives 2-chlorobutane; free-radical chlorination of 2-methylpropane gives mainly the primary chloride because there are nine primary H to one tertiary H.

questions.q: Phenol is treated with bromine dissolved in carbon disulphide (CS₂) at a low temperature. The main products are:
questions.x: In a non-polar solvent at low temperature the ring is less activated (phenol is not ionised) and only one bromine substitutes, at the ortho or para position. Bromine water, a polar solvent, gives the white 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

questions.q: Propanone is shaken with dilute aqueous NaOH (aldol condensation). The addition product is:
questions.x: OH⁻ removes an α-H to give ⁻CH₂COCH₃, which adds to the C=O of another propanone: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂COCH₃. 3-Hydroxybutanal is the aldol of ethanal; propanone has α-hydrogens, so it does not undergo a Cannizzaro-type reaction.

questions.q: Which formula shows the dipeptide in which glycine provides the free –NH₂ end and alanine the free –COOH end?
questions.x: The COOH of glycine condenses with the NH₂ of alanine to form –CO–NH–, leaving glycine's NH₂ and alanine's COOH free. The second formula is the other dipeptide (alanine at the NH₂ end); the ester link –COO– is not a peptide bond.

questions.q: Which two-step route converts ethene into ethanoic acid?
o: Steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst; then acidified K₂Cr₂O₇, distilling off the product as it forms
HBr; then reflux with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
Cold dilute alkaline KMnO₄; then steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst
Steam with H₃PO₄ catalyst; then reflux with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇
questions.x: Hydration gives ethanol, and heating ethanol under reflux with excess oxidant takes it all the way to ethanoic acid. Distilling the product off as it forms stops at ethanal; bromoethane is not oxidised to an acid by dichromate.

questions.q: Kevlar has the repeat unit –CO–C₆H₄–CO–NH–C₆H₄–NH– (both rings 1,4-substituted). Its monomers and type of polymer are:
o: Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and benzene-1,4-diamine; a condensation polyester
Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and benzene-1,4-diol; a condensation polyester
Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid and benzene-1,4-diamine; a condensation polyamide
Phenylethene and acrylonitrile; an addition copolymer
questions.x: Cutting each –CO–NH– link and adding back H₂O gives HOOC–C₆H₄–COOH and H₂N–C₆H₄–NH₂; the links are amide links, so it is a polyamide like nylon. Calling it a polyester confuses –CO–NH– with –CO–O–.

questions.q: Triple superphosphate is made by treating rock phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂, with phosphoric acid instead of sulphuric acid. Compared with ordinary superphosphate, it:
o: Contains insoluble Ca₃(PO₄)₂, so it acts more slowly
Contains nitrogen as well as phosphorus
Contains gypsum, which slows its action in the soil
Contains no calcium sulphate, so it has a higher percentage of phosphorus
questions.x: Ca₃(PO₄)₂ + 4H₃PO₄ → 3Ca(H₂PO₄)₂: no CaSO₄ is formed, so the product is not diluted by gypsum and is richer in phosphorus. Ordinary superphosphate is a mixture of Ca(H₂PO₄)₂ with CaSO₄, which is why the gypsum options are tempting but wrong.

questions.q: Banks read the account and cheque numbers printed in special magnetic ink at the bottom of cheques with which device?
questions.x: MICR reads characters printed with ink containing magnetic particles, which is why banks use it for cheques. An OMR only senses whether marks are present in fixed positions; it does not read magnetic characters.

questions.q: Which of the following is a low-level language?
questions.x: Assembly language uses short codes (mnemonics) that match machine instructions one to one, so it is a low-level language. Python, Java and BASIC are high-level languages written in English-like statements.

questions.q: Which list puts the languages in order from lowest level (closest to the hardware) to highest level?
o: Assembly language, machine language, high-level language
High-level language, assembly language, machine language
Machine language, assembly language, high-level language
Machine language, high-level language, assembly language
questions.x: Machine language is binary code the CPU runs directly, assembly language replaces it with mnemonics, and high-level languages use English-like statements. Putting assembly below machine language reverses the first two levels.

questions.q: Which of the following is written in the form of an IPv6 address?
questions.x: IPv6 addresses are written as groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons, with :: standing for a run of zero groups. 192.168.10.1 is an IPv4 address, and www.example.pk is a domain name.

questions.q: In the IPv4 address 192.168.1.10, the last octet 10 is written in 8-bit binary as:
questions.x: 10 = 8 + 2, so the bits for 8 and 2 are 1: 00001010. 00010000 is 16, which comes from reading "10" as if it were hexadecimal.

questions.q: Four friends share files in a peer-to-peer network. Sara switches her computer off. What happens?
o: Files kept only on Sara's computer cannot be reached; the others still share
The whole network stops, because Sara's computer was the server
Nothing changes, because the files are stored on a central server
All the other computers are switched off automatically
questions.x: In peer-to-peer each computer shares its own resources, so only what is stored on Sara's computer becomes unavailable. There is no central server in peer-to-peer, so the others carry on.

questions.q: Before typing card details into a shopping website, which sign shows that the connection to the site is encrypted?
o: The site has many colourful pictures
The address begins with https:// and shows a padlock
questions.x: https and the padlock mean data between the browser and the site is encrypted. A site's pictures, speed or a .com ending say nothing about encryption.

questions.q: Group members edit a shared report, and the owner wants every change marked so that she can accept or reject each one. Which feature should they use?
questions.x: Track changes, called suggesting mode in some programs, marks each edit for the owner to accept or reject. Version history only lets earlier copies be viewed or restored, not single changes approved.

questions.q: Checking an account balance and paying electricity bills from home through a bank's secure website is called:
questions.x: Internet (online) banking lets customers use bank services through the bank's website or app from anywhere. ATM banking needs the customer to go to a cash machine.

questions.q: In Platform as a Service (PaaS), which part does the customer manage?
o: The physical servers in the data centre
The operating system of the servers
The network cables and storage disks
Its own application code and data
questions.x: In PaaS the provider runs the hardware, operating system and run-time platform, and the customer only builds and manages its own app and data. Managing the operating system is the customer's job only in IaaS.

questions.q: A USB flash drive is formatted. What is the result?
o: Only the viruses on it are removed
Its files are sorted into alphabetical order
The files on it are removed, and it is prepared to store new files
questions.x: Formatting prepares a drive with a fresh file system, so the files on it are lost. It does not sort files, choose only viruses or increase capacity.

questions.q: Folder X holds 3 files and a subfolder Y, and Y holds 2 files. Folder X is copied into an empty folder Z. How many files are now inside Z, counting all its subfolders?
questions.x: Copying a folder copies everything inside it, subfolders included, so Z now holds X with its 3 files and Y with its 2 files, 3 + 2 = 5. The answer 3 forgets the files inside subfolder Y.

questions.q: A sequential master file sorted by account number is updated in a single pass with one day's transactions. What must be done to the transaction file first?
o: Copy it onto a direct-access disk
Remove every account number that appears twice
questions.x: In one pass the master file and the transaction file are read side by side, so both must be in the same key order or matching records would be missed. Date-and-time order is the order the transactions happened, and one account may rightly have several transactions.

questions.q: In the database life cycle, at which step is the ER diagram turned into tables with columns, primary keys and foreign keys for a relational DBMS?
questions.x: Logical design maps the ER model to relations (tables) of the chosen data model. Conceptual design draws the ER diagram itself, and physical design decides storage and indexes.

questions.q: Where does the Form Header section appear when a form is opened in Form view?
o: Above every record shown on the form
Only when the last record is shown
Once at the top of the form, whichever record is shown
At the bottom of every printed page
questions.x: The Form Header is shown once at the top of the form and does not change from record to record, so it suits titles and logos. Data for each record appears in the Detail section.

questions.q: A report on Student(Name, City) is grouped by City in ascending order and sorted by Name within each group. The records are (Sana, Multan), (Ali, Lahore), (Zain, Karachi), (Bilal, Karachi), (Hina, Lahore). In which order are the names printed?
questions.x: Cities in ascending order are Karachi, Lahore, Multan, and names are sorted inside each: Bilal, Zain, then Ali, Hina, then Sana. Sorting by name alone, ignoring the groups, would give Ali first.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
printf("%.3f", 1.0 / 8);
```
questions.x: 1.0 / 8 is a floating-point division giving 0.125, and %.3f prints exactly three decimal places. 0.000 would come from integer division 1 / 8 = 0, which does not happen because 1.0 is not an integer.

questions.q: A program will be run many times without changes. What is an advantage of compiling it rather than running it through an interpreter?
o: Once compiled, it runs without being translated again each time
It can be changed without being translated again
Errors are reported one line at a time while it runs
No translator program is needed at all
questions.x: A compiler translates the whole program once into an executable, which then runs directly and faster. An interpreter must translate the statements again every time the program runs.
add returns 6, but the call is not used in an assignment, so the value is simply thrown away. s itself was passed by value and is never changed, so 1 is printed.
i becomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. When i is 2, continue skips the addition, so s = 1 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 13. continue does not end the loop (that would be break), so 1 is wrong.
For i = 1 the inner loop prints 1, 2, 3; for i = 2 it prints 2, 4, 6. The inner loop finishes all its passes before i changes, so the order 1 2 2 4 3 6 is wrong.

questions.q: Which pair of functions reads and writes formatted data, such as numbers with `%d`, in a text file?
questions.x: fscanf and fprintf work like scanf and printf but take a FILE pointer, so they read and write formatted values in a file. fgetc and fputc handle one character at a time, and scanf/printf use the keyboard and screen.

questions.q:
What happens when this Python code runs?
```
age = 18
print("Age: " + age)
```
o: It is a syntax error at the `+` sign
It stops with a runtime error (TypeError), because a string and an integer cannot be joined with `+`
questions.x: In Python, + between a str and an int raises a TypeError when the line runs; the number must be converted first, as in str(age). The line is written correctly, so it is not a syntax error.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
class Lamp:
    def __init__(self):
        self.on = False
    def switch(self):
        self.on = not self.on
x = Lamp()
y = Lamp()
x.switch()
x.switch()
y.switch()
print(x.on, y.on)
```
questions.x: Each object has its own `on` attribute. x is switched twice (False → True → False) and y once (False → True), so False True. The objects do not share one value.

o: 2 is printed, then an AttributeError occurs
2 and 1 are printed on two lines
1 and 2 are printed on two lines
an AttributeError occurs before anything is printed
questions.x: Child defines its own `__init__` and never calls `super().__init__()`, so Base's `__init__` does not run and `x` is never set. `c.y` prints 2, then `c.x` raises an AttributeError.

questions.q:
What is printed?
```
class Student:
    school = "GC"
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
s = Student("Hira")
print(s.name, s.school)
```
o: an AttributeError, because `school` is not set in `__init__`
questions.x: `school` is a class attribute, shared by all Student objects, so `s.school` finds it in the class: GC. An attribute does not have to be set in `__init__` to be reached through an object.

questions.q: A bubble sort (ascending) makes left-to-right passes of adjacent swaps and stops after the first pass that makes no swap. How many passes does it make on `[1, 2, 3, 5, 4]`?
questions.x: Pass 1 swaps 5 and 4, giving [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The list is now sorted, but the algorithm only knows this after pass 2 makes no swap, so it makes 2 passes. 4 is the count without the early stop.

questions.q: Which of these sorting methods makes at most n − 1 swaps on any list of n elements?
o: Insertion sort done by swapping neighbours
Bubble sort with an early stop
questions.x: Selection sort makes at most one swap per pass and needs n − 1 passes. Bubble sort (with or without early stop) and neighbour-swapping insertion sort can need about n²/2 swaps on a reversed list.

questions.q: Algorithm X takes n² steps and algorithm Y takes 100n steps on an input of size n. For n = 50, which takes fewer steps?
o: Y, because an O(n) algorithm always takes fewer steps
Both take the same number of steps
questions.x: X: 50² = 2,500; Y: 100 × 50 = 5,000, so X is faster here. Big-O describes growth for large n: Y wins only when n > 100, not for every n.

questions.q: Which of these measures the spread of a data set rather than its centre?
questions.x: The range (largest value minus smallest) shows how spread out the data is. Mean, median and mode are all measures of the centre (central tendency).

questions.q: The writer's main purpose in the passage is to:
o: explain how shopkeepers can attract more customers to their shops
argue that cars should be kept out of market streets altogether
describe how cities decide where to build new car parks
argue that charging for street parking would make busy streets work better
questions.x: The writer argues that free parking causes crowding and that "A modest charge ... would change behaviour". Banning cars is wrong: the charge works "without banning anyone" and "None of this is a war on motorists".

questions.q: According to the passage, who often fills the spaces outside shops on a street with free parking?
o: Customers making quick visits to the shops
Delivery vans unloading goods for the market
A few early arrivals, sometimes the shopkeepers themselves
questions.x: The spaces "are often filled all day by a few early arrivals, sometimes the shopkeepers themselves". Quick visits are what a charge would make room for, not what happens now.

questions.q: The writer's argument implies that the main cost of free parking falls on:
o: drivers, who must buy extra fuel while circling
the town, which must pay to build new car parks
people who could have used the street space in other ways
shopkeepers, who must pay rent for the spaces outside
questions.x: Someone pays for the space, "only not the driver": the land could have held a footpath, a cart, a bus stop or trees, and pedestrians "have long been denied" good pavements. Drivers are wrong because the writer says plainly that they are not the ones who pay.

questions.q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "curious" most nearly means:
questions.x: A gift that is paid for by someone other than the giver or the receiver is a "curious kind of gift", that is, a strange one. "Eager to learn" is the commoner meaning, used of people, not of a gift.

questions.q: Which best describes the writer's tone in the last paragraph?
o: Reasonable and reassuring, stressing that the plan is fair
Angry and hostile towards car owners
Doubtful and hesitant about the proposal
questions.x: The writer calls the charge "modest", says "None of this is a war on motorists" and asks only for "a fair share". Hostility is ruled out by that very sentence about motorists.

questions.q: The passage is mainly about:
o: why reinforced concrete is the best material for every home
low-cost ways of making village houses less likely to collapse in earthquakes
how engineers predict when earthquakes will strike
why stone houses in the mountains last only a few years
questions.x: After describing why stone houses fall, the passage gives "cheaper ways to hold a building together". Concrete is called "out of reach for most families", and stone houses stand "for decades".

questions.q: Why, according to the passage, do the stone houses described fail in a strong earthquake?
o: Their roofs are too light to hold the walls in place
The ground beneath them sinks during the shaking
Years of ordinary use have already cracked their walls
The quake pushes them sideways and their loosely joined walls come apart
questions.x: A quake "pushes it sideways, back and forth, and the loose walls simply peel apart". The roofs are "thick" and "heavy", not light.

questions.q: The remark that "concrete poorly made can be deadlier than stone" suggests that:
o: stone is always a safer material than concrete
a stronger material is of little help unless it is used with skill
concrete should never be used in mountain villages
families prefer stone because it looks traditional
questions.x: The danger lies in concrete "poorly made", so the material is only as good as the work. "Always safer" goes too far: the passage calls concrete "the obvious answer" and objects only to its cost and to bad workmanship.

questions.q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "modest" most nearly means:
o: limited in what it tries to do
questions.x: The aim is not a "quake-proof" house but one that stands "long enough for the people inside to get out", so modest means limited. Being shy about one's success is the word's commoner meaning for people.

questions.q: In the first paragraph, the words "Such a house" refer to a house:
o: of stacked stones and mud mortar with a thick, flat roof
with bands of timber running through its walls
already damaged by an earlier earthquake
questions.x: The sentence before describes houses "made of heavy stones stacked with weak mud mortar and topped with a thick, flat roof". Timber bands are one of the improvements described later.
